narrative: The model estimated a 12% chance that you will fail the final year. That is a low probability, but under the school’s rule it is treated as enough risk to require remedial courses, so the decision is precautionary rather than a certainty; your age, sex and health were not used. The strongest influence was your record of no past class failures, which pushes the estimate toward passing. Your low weekend alcohol use was the second strongest factor and also protective, and your good family relationships—the most common rating among students who passed—were third, again lowering risk. So the top-ranked information is mainly reassuring, which explains why the estimated failure risk is only 12%; the remaining risk comes from weaker combined signals rather than one clear warning sign. Those include living with more than three family members, parents living apart, parents whose education ended at primary level, a mother and father working at home, no family educational support, no paid classes, very high free time and going out, and being in a romantic relationship. Your study time of 2–5 hours, low absences (2 versus an average near 3.8), and wish to continue to higher education are positives. To improve, keep attendance steady, use remedial sessions to build a fixed weekly study plan, reduce very high free-time and going-out distractions, and ask school staff or family for structured support.
